cards.front: {{c1::Natural selection}} is the process in which individuals with some inherited traits survive and reproduce more than others.
cards.quote: Natural selection is the process in which individuals with some inherited traits survive and reproduce more than others.
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: What three conditions must a population meet for natural selection to act?
cards.back: Variation among individuals, inheritance of the differences, and unequal reproductive success (the differences change how many reproducing offspring an individual leaves).
cards.quote: Unequal reproductive success: the differences change how many reproducing offspring an individual leaves.
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: {{c1::Fitness}} is how many offspring an individual leaves that survive to reproduce.
cards.quote: Fitness is how many offspring an individual leaves that survive to reproduce.
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: Why does high fitness in biology not simply mean being strong?
cards.back: Fitness counts surviving offspring. A strong animal that leaves no young has a fitness of zero.
cards.quote: Fitness does not mean strength: a strong animal that leaves no young has a fitness of zero.
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: An {{c1::adaptation}} is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its present environment.
cards.quote: An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its present environment.
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: A {{c1::mutation}} is a change in DNA and the source of new versions of genes.
cards.quote: A mutation is a change in DNA and the source of new versions of genes; sexual reproduction shuffles them
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: On Daphne Major in 1977, why was a deep beak an adaptation for medium ground finches?
cards.back: After the drought the seeds left were large and hard. Birds with large, deep beaks could crack them and survived best.
cards.quote: Large birds, especially males with large beaks, survived best because they could crack the large, hard seeds left after the drought.
cards.section: How natural selection changes a population

cards.front: In a finch model, every starting bird has the same inherited beak depth. Can selection favour one beak depth over another?
cards.back: No. The environment may kill birds, but without inherited variation in beak depth it cannot sort birds by that trait. Mutation may later add new variation.
cards.quote: No. The environment may kill birds, but without inherited variation in beak depth, it cannot sort birds by that trait.
cards.section: Explore: test the model

cards.front: In a finch model, selection by large, hard seeds has pushed mean beak depth up. The seed supply then switches to small, soft seeds. Which way is the mean likely to move?
cards.back: It is likely to stop rising and move back toward shallower beaks. The rule: when the environment changes, selection can push in a new direction.
cards.quote: and when the environment changes, selection can push in a new direction.

cards.front: After the 1977 drought the surviving finches had deeper beaks on average. Did the drought reshape the birds' beaks, or change which birds were left?
cards.back: It changed which birds were left. The deeper beaks were measured before the drought, so the groups differed from the start.
cards.quote: The survivors had deeper beaks on average.

cards.front: Before the drought, nonsurvivors had a mean beak depth of 9.11 mm and survivors 9.67 mm in a sample of medium ground finches. How much deeper, on average, were the survivors' beaks?
cards.back: 9.67 mm minus 9.11 mm = 0.56 mm deeper on average.
cards.why: A mean difference compares the groups; it does not say every deep-beaked bird lived.
cards.quote: Subtract the two means. How much deeper, on average, were the survivors' beaks?
cards.section: Read the drought data

cards.front: In the drought table of 100 medium ground finches, in which beak-depth range do survivors first outnumber nonsurvivors?
cards.back: From 9.5 to under 10.0 mm (9 survivors against 8 nonsurvivors). Survivors also outnumber nonsurvivors in every larger range.
cards.quote: From 9.5 to under 10.0 mm, survivors first outnumber nonsurvivors.
cards.section: Read the drought data

cards.front: Why is the claim "every deep-beaked finch survived the drought" wrong, given the table?
cards.back: The groups overlap. Some deep-beaked birds were nonsurvivors (4 in the 10.0 to under 10.5 mm range), so no single beak depth guarantees survival.
cards.quote: The groups still overlap, so no single beak depth guarantees survival.
cards.section: Read the drought data

cards.front: The drought table holds 50 survivors and 50 nonsurvivors. Does it show that half of the island's finches survived?
cards.back: No. The sample was built to contain equal groups, so the 50-50 split is not the island's survival rate. It can only compare beak measurements between the two groups.
cards.quote: The sample was built to contain equal groups, so its 50–50 split is not the island's survival rate.
cards.section: Read the drought data

cards.front: Does selection make a population perfectly suited to its environment?
cards.back: No. It makes the population better suited, not perfectly suited. The Grants also saw its direction change more than once as rainfall and seeds changed.
cards.quote: Selection makes a population better suited to its environment, but not perfectly suited.
cards.section: Read the drought data

cards.front: What is a species under the biological species concept?
cards.back: A group of populations whose members interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, while rarely breeding with other groups.
cards.quote: a group of populations whose members interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, while rarely breeding with other groups.
cards.section: From population change to a species split

cards.front: Name two limits of the biological species concept.
cards.back: It works only for organisms that reproduce sexually, and its edges are fuzzy: Darwin's finch species on Daphne Major still hybridise now and then.
cards.quote: It works only for organisms that reproduce sexually, and its edges are fuzzy.
cards.section: From population change to a species split

cards.front: What is gene flow?
cards.back: The movement of gene versions between populations when individuals, or sex cells such as pollen, arrive and add their genes.
cards.quote: Gene flow moves gene versions between populations when individuals, or sex cells such as pollen, arrive and add their genes.
cards.section: From population change to a species split

cards.front: Why can geographic isolation start the formation of a new species?
cards.back: A river, mountain range or canyon separates populations and reduces gene flow, so each group can change on its own.
cards.quote: A split often begins with geographic isolation, when a river, mountain range or canyon separates populations and reduces gene flow.
cards.section: From population change to a species split

cards.front: Squirrels north of the Grand Canyon look different from those to the south. Do the looks alone show they are two species?
cards.back: No. Interbreeding is the test. Biologists usually treat the northern Kaibab squirrel as a subspecies of Abert's squirrel, so as one species.
cards.quote: Yet biologists usually treat it as a subspecies of Abert's squirrel, so as one species.
cards.section: What the simple split leaves out

cards.front: What is hybrid speciation, and how did it show up on Daphne Major?
cards.back: Two species give rise to a third. An immigrant male bred with a resident medium ground finch, and the hybrid descendants stopped breeding with the island's other finches within three generations.
cards.quote: This special case, in which two species give rise to a third, is hybrid speciation.
cards.section: What the simple split leaves out

cards.front: Why can antibiotic resistance spread in days while change in large animals takes decades?
cards.back: How fast selection shifts a population depends partly on how fast generations turn over. Bacteria divide often; large animals do not.
cards.quote: Natural selection can shift a population within days or over millions of years, depending partly on how fast generations turn over.
cards.section: Fast change, slow change and extinction

cards.front: In {{c1::punctuated equilibrium}}, species stay much the same for most of their history, and most change comes in bursts when new species branch.
cards.quote: Species stay much the same for most of their history; most change comes in bursts when new species branch, bursts that are fast in geologic time
cards.section: Fast change, slow change and extinction

cards.front: Compare gradualism with punctuated equilibrium, and give the picture for each.
cards.back: Gradualism: small changes add up steadily over long periods (a ramp). Punctuated equilibrium: long stability, then change in bursts at branching (a staircase).
cards.quote: Small changes add up steadily over long periods
cards.section: Fast change, slow change and extinction

cards.front: A fossil lineage shows a geologically short burst of change. Is that the same as the fast change seen in bacteria or elephants?
cards.back: No. A geologically short burst can still last thousands of years. Both patterns can also occur in one lineage at different times.
cards.quote: A geologically short burst can still last thousands of years, so it is not the same as fast change in bacteria or elephants.
cards.section: Fast change, slow change and extinction

cards.front: A finch population becomes better suited to its island over many generations, yet the species dies out. How can both be true?
cards.back: Adaptation does not guarantee rescue. If the environment worsens faster than the population changes, it can be better suited and still shrink to nothing (extinction).
cards.quote: A population can become better suited and still shrink to nothing if its environment worsens faster than it changes.
cards.section: Fast change, slow change and extinction

cards.front: Banded finches are measured before a drought, and survivors have deeper beaks afterward. What further measurement would show the change was inherited?
cards.back: Measure the survivors' young. A higher mean beak depth in them, with young resembling their parents, is evidence the change was inherited. Without it, the data show only who survived.
cards.quote: A higher mean in them, with young resembling their parents, is evidence that the change was inherited.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why compare a drought year with a wet year when testing whether drought selects on beak depth?
cards.back: A wet year is the comparison. If beak depth predicts survival only in the drought, drought conditions are a stronger explanation.
cards.quote: If beak depth predicts survival only during the drought, selection by drought conditions becomes a stronger explanation.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a study of beak depth and drought survival, which is the independent variable and which is the dependent variable?
cards.back: Beak depth is the independent variable; survival is the dependent variable.
cards.quote: Beak depth is the independent variable and survival the dependent variable.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A river splits a finch population in two, and each side faces different seeds. Explain how selection and isolation together could produce two species, and what shows the split is complete.
cards.back: With little gene flow, each side is selected toward different traits. The split is complete when barriers prevent interbreeding or allow only rare hybrids; then the groups count as separate species.
cards.quote: If barriers prevent interbreeding, or allow only rare hybrids, the groups count as separate species.
cards.section: What the simple split leaves out
